entries.title: Chaela of the Exiled School
entries.body:
Chaela organized lessons after escaping a failed assembly. Her earlier public certainty contrasts with cautious later supply accounts. Schools preserve both phases, allowing change without treating survival as proof that every past decision was wise.

Later accounts make Chaela of the Exiled School the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Lessons After the Sea King. One sea king inherited three coastal crowns without uniting their separate laws. His death in 156 divided the union and left harbor households facing rival claims. A later campaign targeted a named coastal population as presumed supporters of rebellion, destroying villages and making survival dependent on boats maintained outside royal patronage. An exiled student organizer built schools for displaced children, while a composer arranged progressively difficult reed-lute lessons around names and places survivors wanted retained. The music was teachable to beginners rather than reserved for famous virtuosi. Present schools preserve the repertoire alongside factual testimony, distinguishing remembrance through performance from evidence needed to establish responsibility for particular losses.

In the connected record, [The Three Crown Landing](b030-the-three-crown-landing.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Learner’s Refusal Right](b030-the-learner-s-refusal-right.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether schools can keep testimony and useful teaching accessible without turning survivors’ names into exclusive property of a commemorative patron.

entries.title: The Three Crown Landing
entries.body:
Three carved crowns share a quay whose working agreements never became uniform. Visitors assume one vanished empire. Pilots distinguish separate landing rights, explaining why the ruler’s death divided political title more quickly than everyday cooperation.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Progressive Lesson Houses
entries.body:
Beginners learn short measures before elaborate works. Patrons want impressive public recitals only. Teachers keep modest lessons because the repertoire’s survival depends on many ordinary learners, not a few virtuosi carrying every name.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Named Coast Campaign
entries.body:
Officials classified a whole population as supporting revolt and attacked civilian settlements. Surviving accounts distinguish military resistance from ordinary residence. That distinction preserves responsibility without requiring every harmed household to share one political allegiance.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Beginner’s Reed Lute
entries.body:
A small instrument uses replaceable reeds and a repaired neck suited to young hands. Its simplicity supports wide teaching. Commemorative patrons offer ornate models difficult to maintain, confusing visible honor with what pupils actually need.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Name Learned Slowly
entries.body:
Teachers explain a carried name before adding it to a musical exercise. Learners may decline public performance. The custom prevents remembrance from making children responsible for displaying grief they have not chosen or understood.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Studies of Returning Harbors
entries.body:
The studies progress through increasingly difficult intervals associated with lost landing places. They do not reproduce complete testimony. Teachers pair them with separate factual accounts, preserving music’s mnemonic usefulness without treating a melody as sufficient evidence of a particular act.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Black Shore Porpoise
entries.body:
Porpoises follow seasonal fish routes beyond crown boundaries. Rescue crews learned currents by watching them but cannot command their movements. Keeping this limitation visible prevents a useful observation becoming a legend of animals guaranteeing safe passage.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Boats Beyond Patronage
entries.body:
Independent boat households supplied escape routes when royal services failed. Their accounts document both rescue and passengers they could not carry. Honest remembrance preserves finite courage rather than an impossible story that everybody seeking help was saved.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Learner’s Refusal Right
entries.body:
A child may learn practical music without publicly reciting inherited loss. Schools separate education from commemorative obligation. Patrons resist because performances attract donations, exposing a dependency that must be funded without making vulnerable pupils its instruments.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Sea King’s Last Division
entries.body:
The king’s death activated separate succession rules despite his shared titles. Court histories blame disloyal heirs. Local agreements reveal that the union never included a witnessed undertaking merging all harbor law, making division less surprising than later epics suggest.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Three Harbor Teaching Board
entries.body:
The board contains beginner marks from all three coasts. One patron wants its least prestigious repairs removed. Teachers retain them because they document continued use after the union broke, the material history that gives the object its significance.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Rescue Portion Remembered
entries.body:
Schools cook one meal measured to an actual rescue boat’s supplies. Additional guests receive ordinary separately recorded food. The distinction prevents a finite historical portion from being romanticized into miraculous provision while keeping hospitality open.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Campaign’s Civilian Inventories
entries.body:
Inventories record tools, food stores, gardens, and households destroyed. Military histories dismiss them as possessions rather than strategy. Readers use them to establish the civilian scope of harm and practical losses requiring restitution.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Lesson Heard Without a Player
entries.body:
A short beginner measure recurs near a school basin after a promised lesson is withheld. Window reeds reproduce part of the sound. Teachers provide the finite instruction owed and continue observation, refusing to use uncertainty as a reason to neglect a child.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Reed Lute Repair Teaching
entries.body:
Pupils learn simple repairs alongside playing, using local materials. The practice reduces dependence on distant patrons. It also gives the musical tradition a practical future beyond commemorative funding that may end when public attention moves elsewhere.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Patron’s Exclusive Repertoire
entries.body:
A donor claims exclusive rights to public lessons carrying survivor names. Teachers offer acknowledgment but reject perpetual control. The hearing distinguishes funding useful work from acquiring authority over people and histories the donor did not create.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
